text: The horrible cry in the night
why: ¶238 describes 'the most horrible cry to which I have ever listened'.

text: The sleepers in the village and the parsonage
why: ¶238 says the cry raised the sleepers in the village and even in the distant parsonage.

text: The thing at which Holmes lashes
why: ¶238 says Holmes lashed furiously with his cane at the bell-pull; Watson could not see what it was, so the label is only a neutral descriptor.

text: That instant: Holmes strikes a match, and Watson hears a low, clear whistle
why: ¶238: 'At the moment when Holmes struck the light I heard a low, clear whistle.'

text: A moment later: Holmes has ceased to strike and gazes up at the ventilator, pale with horror
why: ¶238: Holmes 'had ceased to strike and was gazing up at the ventilator'; his face was 'deadly pale and filled with horror and loathing'.

text: Then: a most horrible cry breaks from the silence of the night
why: ¶238 describes the most horrible cry breaking from the silence of the night, directly after the preceding moment.

text: What they say in the village
why: ¶238: 'They say that away down in the village... that cry raised the sleepers from their beds.'

text: What was the whistle for? — to call the thing back when a light showed in the room
id: q.whistle_for=to call the thing back when a light showed in the room
why: The whistle is a central unexplained clue, and the story has linked it to animals (the baboon, cheetah, gipsies, 'speckled band'), so a signal to a creature is a possibility a reader has reason to consider.

text: What will happen in the middle room to-night? — harm comes to Dr. Roylott himself
id: q.tonight=harm comes to Dr. Roylott himself
why: The story so far places the danger on Helen, who occupies the middle room; nothing suggests Roylott himself will be harmed there.
A plain question about the cry just heard, not worded to point at an answer.

text: Who made the low whistle in the night? — it sounded the moment a light was struck in a shuttered room, a light that could be seen only through the ventilator
why: The whistle sounded at the moment of Holmes's match, and Holmes had said the light could be seen only through the ventilator (¶229).

text: Where did the whistle come from? — it answered a light in a shuttered room that could be seen only through the ventilator
why: The whistle coincided with the struck light, which Holmes had said could be seen only through the ventilator. 'Answered' is interpretive but matches the timing.

text: What was the whistle for? — it sounded the moment a light was struck that could be seen through the ventilator
why: The whistle sounded the moment the light was struck, and the question about its purpose is one the story gives reason to ask.

text: What was Holmes lashing at on the bell-pull? — it made a gentle sound like steam from a kettle, and left Holmes pale with horror and loathing
why: The hissing sound came before Holmes lashed at the bell-pull, but the story never says the thing he lashed at made that sound; Watson could not see it.

text: What, if anything, came through the ventilator into that room? — a low, clear whistle sounds at the moment it is on the bell-pull
why: The story never says anything came through the ventilator or was on the bell-pull at the moment of the whistle; Watson saw nothing.
